questions.question: In the Frontier Molecular Orbital analysis of Chapter 24 transformations, what interaction dictates reactivity?

options.label: A
options.text: Overlap between two filled HOMOs.

options.label: B
options.text: Constructive overlap between the HOMO of the electron donor (nucleophile) and the LUMO of the electron acceptor (electrophile) in Chapter 24.

options.label: C
options.text: Repulsion between core 1s electrons.

options.label: D
options.text: Overlap between two empty LUMOs.

questions.correct_answer: Constructive overlap between the HOMO of the electron donor (nucleophile) and the LUMO of the electron acceptor (electrophile) in Chapter 24.
questions.explanation: Chemical reactions are governed by HOMO-LUMO frontier orbital interactions that maximize constructive bonding overlap.

questions.question: According to the Woodward-Hoffmann rules, what condition allows a thermal pericyclic reaction in Chapter 24?

options.label: A
options.text: The reaction must proceed with 100% loss of entropy.

options.label: B
options.text: Conservation of orbital symmetry: the symmetry of the reactant molecular orbitals must correlate continuously with ground-state product orbitals in Chapter 24.

options.label: C
options.text: The reaction must generate free radicals.

options.label: D
options.text: The reaction must be heated to over 1000°C.

questions.correct_answer: Conservation of orbital symmetry: the symmetry of the reactant molecular orbitals must correlate continuously with ground-state product orbitals in Chapter 24.
questions.explanation: Thermally allowed pericyclic processes proceed through transition states where orbital phase symmetry is conserved without crossing high-energy antibonding levels.

questions.question: What is the difference between suprafacial and antarafacial orbital participation in Chapter 24 cycloadditions?

options.label: A
options.text: Both terms mean identical facial attack.

options.label: B
options.text: Suprafacial requires breaking all single bonds.

options.label: C
options.text: Antarafacial occurs only in the gas phase.

options.label: D
options.text: Suprafacial reactions involve bonding on the SAME face of the π system at both termini; antarafacial involves bonding on OPPOSITE faces in Chapter 24.

questions.correct_answer: Suprafacial reactions involve bonding on the SAME face of the π system at both termini; antarafacial involves bonding on OPPOSITE faces in Chapter 24.
questions.explanation: Suprafacial processes engage the same face (top-top or bottom-bottom); antarafacial processes engage opposite faces of the participating π component.

questions.topic: Ch24 Electrocyclic Ring Closure Conrotatory Selection
questions.question: For a thermal [4n] π-electron electrocyclic reaction in Chapter 24, what motion is symmetry-allowed?

options.label: A
options.text: Disrotatory motion (rotating in opposite directions).

options.label: B
options.text: Conrotatory motion (both terminal p orbitals rotate in the SAME direction) dictated by opposite phase signs in the HOMO in Chapter 24.

options.label: C
options.text: Planar translation without rotation.

options.label: D
options.text: Complete dissociation into atoms.

questions.correct_answer: Conrotatory motion (both terminal p orbitals rotate in the SAME direction) dictated by opposite phase signs in the HOMO in Chapter 24.
questions.explanation: Thermal 4n electrocyclic reactions require conrotatory rotation to bring terminal lobes into constructive in-phase overlap.

questions.question: Why does photochemical excitation switch the allowed electrocyclic pathway to disrotatory in Chapter 24?

options.label: A
options.text: Light eliminates all orbital nodes.

options.label: B
options.text: Photons destroy the carbon framework.

options.label: C
options.text: Photons heat the solvent to 500°C.

options.label: D
options.text: Light promotes an electron to the next higher orbital (ψ_{n+1}*), inverting the terminal orbital symmetry of the new HOMO in Chapter 24.

questions.correct_answer: Light promotes an electron to the next higher orbital (ψ_{n+1}*), inverting the terminal orbital symmetry of the new HOMO in Chapter 24.
questions.explanation: Photochemical excitation inverts the orbital symmetry of the HOMO, switching the selection rule from conrotatory to disrotatory (or vice versa).

questions.question: What quantum mechanical effect accounts for endo selectivity in Chapter 24 [4+2] cycloadditions?

options.label: A
options.text: Steric repulsion between alkyl groups.

options.label: B
options.text: Favorable secondary orbital overlap between the developing diene π system and the electron-withdrawing dienophile substituent in Chapter 24.

options.label: C
options.text: Dipole cancellation in nonpolar solvents.

options.label: D
options.text: Electrostatic repulsion between nuclei.

questions.correct_answer: Favorable secondary orbital overlap between the developing diene π system and the electron-withdrawing dienophile substituent in Chapter 24.
questions.explanation: Secondary orbital overlap between non-bonding portions of the interacting π systems lowers the transition state energy for the endo pathway.

questions.question: Why is the [4π_s + 2π_s] Diels-Alder cycloaddition thermally allowed in Chapter 24?

options.label: A
options.text: It proceeds via an antiaromatic 8-electron transition state.

options.label: B
options.text: It involves 6 π electrons (a Hückel-type [4n+2] system, n=1) with suprafacial-suprafacial overlap and zero phase inversions in Chapter 24.

options.label: C
options.text: It involves 4 π electrons.

options.label: D
options.text: It requires UV light initiation.

questions.correct_answer: It involves 6 π electrons (a Hückel-type [4n+2] system, n=1) with suprafacial-suprafacial overlap and zero phase inversions in Chapter 24.
questions.explanation: A suprafacial 6π electron transition state is aromatic and thermally allowed by the Woodward-Hoffmann rules.

questions.question: Why does the [2+2] cycloaddition of two alkenes require photochemical excitation (hν) in Chapter 24?

options.label: A
options.text: Alkenes cannot collide in the dark.

options.label: B
options.text: Thermal [2_s + 2_s] is symmetry-forbidden (4n antiaromatic TS); photochemical excitation populates the π* orbital, making [2_s + 2_s] symmetry-allowed in Chapter 24.

options.label: C
options.text: Light changes the alkene into an alkyne.

options.label: D
options.text: Thermal [2+2] requires liquid nitrogen.

questions.correct_answer: Thermal [2_s + 2_s] is symmetry-forbidden (4n antiaromatic TS); photochemical excitation populates the π* orbital, making [2_s + 2_s] symmetry-allowed in Chapter 24.
questions.explanation: Thermal [2s+2s] has mismatched orbital phases (symmetry forbidden); photochemical excitation enables constructive orbital overlap.

questions.question: What is the orbital topology of the transition state in the thermal [3,3]-sigmatropic rearrangement in Chapter 24?

options.label: A
options.text: A stepwise diradical intermediate.

options.label: B
options.text: An open-chain carbocation-carbanion pair.

options.label: C
options.text: A concerted, aromatic 6-electron chair-like transition state with suprafacial-suprafacial orbital overlap across both allylic fragments in Chapter 24.

options.label: D
options.text: A boat transition state with 4 electrons.

questions.correct_answer: A concerted, aromatic 6-electron chair-like transition state with suprafacial-suprafacial orbital overlap across both allylic fragments in Chapter 24.
questions.explanation: Thermal [3,3]-sigmatropic shifts (Cope, Claisen) proceed suprafacially on both 3-carbon fragments via an aromatic 6π transition state.

questions.question: In unsymmetrical pericyclic reactions in Chapter 24, how do substituents govern regioselectivity?

options.label: A
options.text: By converting all bonds to ionic bonds.

options.label: B
options.text: By preventing orbital overlap.

options.label: C
options.text: Electron-donating and electron-withdrawing groups perturb FMO coefficients, directing union between the atom with the largest HOMO coefficient and the largest LUMO coefficient in Chapter 24.

options.label: D
options.text: By increasing the molecular weight of the product.

questions.correct_answer: Electron-donating and electron-withdrawing groups perturb FMO coefficients, directing union between the atom with the largest HOMO coefficient and the largest LUMO coefficient in Chapter 24.
questions.explanation: Substituents polarize FMO coefficients; the fastest reaction occurs by pairing the largest terminal coefficients of the HOMO and LUMO.

options.label: A
options.text: Thermal [2+2] requires liquid nitrogen.

options.label: B
options.text: Thermal [2_s + 2_s] is symmetry-forbidden (4n antiaromatic TS); photochemical excitation populates the π* orbital, making [2_s + 2_s] symmetry-allowed in Chapter 24.

options.label: C
options.text: Light changes the alkene into an alkyne.

options.label: D
options.text: Alkenes cannot collide in the dark.

questions.correct_answer: Thermal [2_s + 2_s] is symmetry-forbidden (4n antiaromatic TS); photochemical excitation populates the π* orbital, making [2_s + 2_s] symmetry-allowed in Chapter 24.
questions.explanation: Thermal [2s+2s] has mismatched orbital phases (symmetry forbidden); photochemical excitation enables constructive orbital overlap.

questions.question: What is the orbital topology of the transition state in the thermal [3,3]-sigmatropic rearrangement in Chapter 24?

options.label: A
options.text: An open-chain carbocation-carbanion pair.

options.label: B
options.text: A stepwise diradical intermediate.

options.label: C
options.text: A concerted, aromatic 6-electron chair-like transition state with suprafacial-suprafacial orbital overlap across both allylic fragments in Chapter 24.

options.label: D
options.text: A boat transition state with 4 electrons.

questions.correct_answer: A concerted, aromatic 6-electron chair-like transition state with suprafacial-suprafacial orbital overlap across both allylic fragments in Chapter 24.
questions.explanation: Thermal [3,3]-sigmatropic shifts (Cope, Claisen) proceed suprafacially on both 3-carbon fragments via an aromatic 6π transition state.

questions.question: In unsymmetrical pericyclic reactions in Chapter 24, how do substituents govern regioselectivity?

options.label: A
options.text: By increasing the molecular weight of the product.

options.label: B
options.text: By preventing orbital overlap.

options.label: C
options.text: By converting all bonds to ionic bonds.

options.label: D
options.text: Electron-donating and electron-withdrawing groups perturb FMO coefficients, directing union between the atom with the largest HOMO coefficient and the largest LUMO coefficient in Chapter 24.

questions.correct_answer: Electron-donating and electron-withdrawing groups perturb FMO coefficients, directing union between the atom with the largest HOMO coefficient and the largest LUMO coefficient in Chapter 24.
questions.explanation: Substituents polarize FMO coefficients; the fastest reaction occurs by pairing the largest terminal coefficients of the HOMO and LUMO.

questions.question: In the Frontier Molecular Orbital analysis of Chapter 24 transformations, what interaction dictates reactivity?

options.label: A
options.text: Overlap between two empty LUMOs.

options.label: B
options.text: Overlap between two filled HOMOs.

options.label: C
options.text: Constructive overlap between the HOMO of the electron donor (nucleophile) and the LUMO of the electron acceptor (electrophile) in Chapter 24.

options.label: D
options.text: Repulsion between core 1s electrons.

questions.correct_answer: Constructive overlap between the HOMO of the electron donor (nucleophile) and the LUMO of the electron acceptor (electrophile) in Chapter 24.
questions.explanation: Chemical reactions are governed by HOMO-LUMO frontier orbital interactions that maximize constructive bonding overlap.

questions.question: According to the Woodward-Hoffmann rules, what condition allows a thermal pericyclic reaction in Chapter 24?

options.label: A
options.text: Conservation of orbital symmetry: the symmetry of the reactant molecular orbitals must correlate continuously with ground-state product orbitals in Chapter 24.

options.label: B
options.text: The reaction must generate free radicals.

options.label: C
options.text: The reaction must proceed with 100% loss of entropy.

options.label: D
options.text: The reaction must be heated to over 1000°C.

questions.correct_answer: Conservation of orbital symmetry: the symmetry of the reactant molecular orbitals must correlate continuously with ground-state product orbitals in Chapter 24.
questions.explanation: Thermally allowed pericyclic processes proceed through transition states where orbital phase symmetry is conserved without crossing high-energy antibonding levels.

questions.question: What is the difference between suprafacial and antarafacial orbital participation in Chapter 24 cycloadditions?

options.label: A
options.text: Suprafacial reactions involve bonding on the SAME face of the π system at both termini; antarafacial involves bonding on OPPOSITE faces in Chapter 24.

options.label: B
options.text: Suprafacial requires breaking all single bonds.

options.label: C
options.text: Antarafacial occurs only in the gas phase.

options.label: D
options.text: Both terms mean identical facial attack.

questions.correct_answer: Suprafacial reactions involve bonding on the SAME face of the π system at both termini; antarafacial involves bonding on OPPOSITE faces in Chapter 24.
questions.explanation: Suprafacial processes engage the same face (top-top or bottom-bottom); antarafacial processes engage opposite faces of the participating π component.

questions.topic: Ch24 Electrocyclic Ring Closure Conrotatory Selection
questions.question: For a thermal [4n] π-electron electrocyclic reaction in Chapter 24, what motion is symmetry-allowed?

options.label: A
options.text: Disrotatory motion (rotating in opposite directions).

options.label: B
options.text: Complete dissociation into atoms.

options.label: C
options.text: Planar translation without rotation.

options.label: D
options.text: Conrotatory motion (both terminal p orbitals rotate in the SAME direction) dictated by opposite phase signs in the HOMO in Chapter 24.

questions.correct_answer: Conrotatory motion (both terminal p orbitals rotate in the SAME direction) dictated by opposite phase signs in the HOMO in Chapter 24.
questions.explanation: Thermal 4n electrocyclic reactions require conrotatory rotation to bring terminal lobes into constructive in-phase overlap.

questions.question: Why does photochemical excitation switch the allowed electrocyclic pathway to disrotatory in Chapter 24?

options.label: A
options.text: Light promotes an electron to the next higher orbital (ψ_{n+1}*), inverting the terminal orbital symmetry of the new HOMO in Chapter 24.

options.label: B
options.text: Photons destroy the carbon framework.

options.label: C
options.text: Light eliminates all orbital nodes.

options.label: D
options.text: Photons heat the solvent to 500°C.

questions.correct_answer: Light promotes an electron to the next higher orbital (ψ_{n+1}*), inverting the terminal orbital symmetry of the new HOMO in Chapter 24.
questions.explanation: Photochemical excitation inverts the orbital symmetry of the HOMO, switching the selection rule from conrotatory to disrotatory (or vice versa).

questions.question: What quantum mechanical effect accounts for endo selectivity in Chapter 24 [4+2] cycloadditions?

options.label: A
options.text: Dipole cancellation in nonpolar solvents.

options.label: B
options.text: Steric repulsion between alkyl groups.

options.label: C
options.text: Favorable secondary orbital overlap between the developing diene π system and the electron-withdrawing dienophile substituent in Chapter 24.

options.label: D
options.text: Electrostatic repulsion between nuclei.

questions.correct_answer: Favorable secondary orbital overlap between the developing diene π system and the electron-withdrawing dienophile substituent in Chapter 24.
questions.explanation: Secondary orbital overlap between non-bonding portions of the interacting π systems lowers the transition state energy for the endo pathway.
